title: The Moon's Speedy, Falling Secret
markdown:
Sunbeams punched through Theo’s window, brilliant golden fingers. A brand new day had exploded into being. Theo blinked awake, a question tugging at him that had tickled all night.

“Ash! Wake up!”

A blur of dazzling blue scales zipped from under a cool dark mushroom cap. “What’s up, Theo?” Ash chirped, lightning-quick tongue flicking as he scrambled onto the bedside table. “Big news?”

Theo bounced out of bed, feet landing with a soft thud. “I was dreaming about the moon. It’s always up there. A big bright circle. But why doesn’t it just fall down? If I drop a juicy ripe tomato from the highest apple-tree branch, splat. It hits the ground. Why doesn’t the moon go splat on us?”

Ash tilted his head, beady intelligent eyes widening. Blue scales shimmered like tiny sapphires. “That’s a really good question. It’s so big. It looks so heavy. It should make a humongous thump. Imagine that.”

They both pictured it. A giant planet-shaking thump. No, thank you. That would definitely not be good for gardening.

Just then a cheerful percussive bang echoed from the garden. Engineer Mara burst through the back door, wild mop of bright red hair practically sparking. “Good morning, stargazers!” In her hands, a curious rather large contraption. “I’ve got something absolutely amazing to show you.”

Mara’s creation was a big stretchy black fabric hoop, taut, held up by three sturdy gleaming metal legs. Dangling from the centre, suspended by nearly invisible threads, was a small sparkly white ball, shimmering like a tiny captured star.

“This is my Cosmic Climber model. It shows the universe’s secret moves.”

“It looks like a giant trampoline for planets,” Theo breathed.

“Or a super-duper extra-large frisbee for space rocks,” Ash added, zipping in excited circles.

Mara grinned. “You’re both so close. Imagine this black fabric isn’t just fabric. Imagine it’s space itself, stretched out and flat. The hoop is the vastness holding it together. Ready for a science lesson that’s truly out of this world? It’s all about why the moon doesn’t just fall down and cause a gigantic mess.”

With careful hands she placed a slightly heavier blue ball onto the centre of the stretchy fabric. Immediately the fabric dipped, creating a gentle valley.

“See this dip? When something big and heavy, like our Earth, sits in space, it bends the fabric of space around it. That bending, that pull, is gravity.”

Theo watched, mesmerised. He thought of how plants always grew towards the sun. “So Earth is like a big heavy marble on a stretchy blanket, making a deep dip in the middle?”

“Precisely.” She picked up the small sparkly white ball. “Imagine the moon is always trying to move in a perfectly straight line, moving super fast.” She gave the moon-ball a firm controlled sideways push.

The moon-ball did not zoom off. It began to roll and curve around the dip made by the Earth-ball. It did not crash headlong. It did not fly away. It kept going around and around, a perfect constant loop.

“Whoa,” squeaked Ash. “Stuck on a magic invisible racetrack. A cosmic carousel.”

“It isn’t actually stuck. That’s the fantastic part. The moon is falling. See how it’s constantly dipping towards Earth because of that bend? But it’s also moving sideways so fast that by the time it falls a little bit, the Earth has already moved forward underneath it. It keeps missing.”

Theo’s eyes lit up. He thought of the colossal sun and the planets circling it. “So the sun must be like a huge super-heavy bowling ball, bending space even more, and the planets are like smaller faster balls rolling around it, always falling towards the sun but always missing because they’re moving so fast?”

“You’ve got it. That constant falling and missing, that sideways speed that keeps it from crashing — that’s an orbit. The moon is in orbit around Earth. Earth is in orbit around the sun. A never-ending dance.”

Ash performed a joyous victory dance, blue scales flashing. “So the moon isn’t just hanging there. It’s on an incredible non-stop chase. Falling and flying all at once.”

Mara began to pack up the Cosmic Climber, eyes twinkling. “Gravity pulls things together. Speed keeps them from colliding head-on, making those amazing loops. Who knows what other secrets are hiding out there?”

Theo looked at the bright blue sky, then at the empty model. “I’m going to watch the moon tonight. Really watch it. And think about its speedy falling missing orbit.”

With a shared curious grin they turned toward the garden, ready to see what other wonders the day — and the sky — had in store. The adventure stretched out like the endless morning itself.
characters: Theo (a curious gardener), Ash (a sapphire-scaled lizard), Engineer Mara (a cosmic-climber inventor)
